I did not see an explicit call to revoke the refresh token (offline_access scope is requested at line 140), though the logout method is outside the range I read. If sign-out only clears local storage, a refresh token that was extracted earlier stays valid.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who extracted the refresh token (for example through the Android backup in F-10-04) keeps using it after the user signs out.
findings.recommendation: Call the revocation endpoint for the refresh and access tokens on sign-out, and perform end-session at the IdP.
findings.confidence_reason: Finding admits partial reading and no verification; speculative.

findings.title: Full card number and CVV pulled into the client via user-info claims, and exceptions logged raw
findings.description: GetUserInfoAsync maps card_number, card_holder and card_security_number claims into UserInfo (approximately lines 85-90). That holds the CVV in memory in the app, and the data comes from the userinfo endpoint over whatever transport the settings specify (see F-10-03). Exceptions are written with Console.WriteLine or Debug.WriteLine (BasketService.cs line 58, CheckoutViewModel.cs line 131, LoginViewModel.cs line 73), which could include request or response content on the platform log in release builds. HandleResponse in RequestProvider.cs (line 156 onward) reads the error body into exceptions. Whether the bodies carry sensitive data is unverified.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker with logcat or device log access (for example, a malicious app on older Android or a developer-attached device) reads logged exception text. With a rogue or cleartext endpoint, the card data is also exposed in transit.
findings.recommendation: Do not retrieve or hold the CVV client-side. Use tokenized payment methods. Strip sensitive bodies from exceptions and logs in release builds.
findings.confidence_reason: Speculative claim about the CVV in memory; console logging of exceptions is noise.

findings.title: Automatic migration and seeding at startup, with default Postgres credential in appsettings.Development.json
findings.description: AddMigration with UsersSeed runs on every start. appsettings.Development.json holds "Password=yourWeak(!)Password" for the postgres superuser. That is a Development-only file, but it is a committed default credential. ASP.NET Identity default lockout and password options are otherwise unchanged. PasswordSignInAsync uses lockoutOnFailure:true, so lockout is on, and the error message is generic ("Invalid username or password"), so I found no account enumeration. The Challenge/Callback paths validate returnUrl with IsValidReturnUrl.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the Development configuration is used against a reachable Postgres instance, the attacker connects as postgres with the known password and reads or modifies the identity database, including the users' card data.
findings.recommendation: Use a secret store or user-secrets for connection strings, and do not ship an admin password in a committed file.
findings.confidence_reason: Development-only appsettings password and startup migration are noise.

findings.title: Logout without prompt via GET, enabling forced logout from third-party pages
findings.description: ShowLogoutPrompt = false (AccountOptions.cs line 10). AccountController.Logout(string logoutId) (GET) calls BuildLogoutViewModelAsync, which leaves ShowLogoutPrompt false when the user is authenticated and the logout context is null or has ShowSignoutPrompt false. It then calls Logout(vm) directly (the "if (vm.ShowLogoutPrompt == false)" branch). The state-changing action therefore happens on a GET with no anti-forgery check. The POST handler is protected, but the GET path bypasses it. The impact is only forced logout.
findings.exploit_scenario: A third-party site embeds an img tag or iframe pointing to https://identity/Account/Logout and silently signs the victim out of the IdP.
findings.recommendation: Set ShowLogoutPrompt = true, or require a signed logoutId from IdentityServer before logging out.
findings.confidence_reason: GET logout CSRF with forced-logout impact only is a standard, low-value quickstart pattern.

findings.title: Diagnostics page gates on RemoteIpAddress, which is unreliable behind a reverse proxy; it exposes the authenticated user's claims and tokens
findings.description: The controller carries [Authorize], and Index allows 127.0.0.1, ::1 or the server's own LocalIpAddress (lines 13-17). If a proxy forwards requests from the same host or loopback, the check passes for every external user. In a container setup, the proxy and Identity API are commonly on the same host or network. DiagnosticsViewModel renders the AuthenticateResult properties (claims and tokens) of the current user. It does not reveal other users' data, so the impact is limited to self-disclosure.
findings.exploit_scenario: Low impact. An authenticated user views their own tokens and claims, which they already hold.
findings.recommendation: Remove the Diagnostics controller outside Development.
findings.confidence_reason: Self-disclosure only, behind [Authorize], and the proxy bypass is speculative.

findings.title: Committed DB superuser password "yourWeak(!)Password" in Development appsettings of 5 services, which are activated by committed launch profiles
findings.description: The password appears in Identity.API/appsettings.Development.json line 3, Catalog.API/appsettings.Development.json line 3, Ordering.API/appsettings.Development.json line 3, Webhooks.API/appsettings.Development.json line 10 and OrderProcessor/appsettings.Development.json line 10. Each is a Host=localhost Username=postgres connection string. The launchSettings profiles set ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development (Catalog.API http profile; AppHost https profile also sets DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT=Development). That turns on the Development-only features: Scalar API UI and the root redirect (OpenApi.Extensions.cs lines 26-41), the /health and /alive endpoints (ServiceDefaults/Extensions.cs lines 115-125), always-on tracing, and the Identity HomeController dev branches (lines 26 and 49). The credential applies only to a local database, so impact depends on whether a developer's Postgres is exposed. If the Development environment is used in a shared or deployed environment, the password is trivially known.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who reaches a Postgres on port 5432 that was started with this password gets superuser access. A deployment started with ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development exposes extra endpoints and uses this committed credential.
findings.recommendation: Remove the credentials from the committed files and use user-secrets or Aspire-injected connection strings. Make sure launch profiles are never used in deployed environments.
findings.confidence_reason: Dev-only appsettings.Development.json password pointing at localhost. This is a test/dev fixture pattern with low impact.

findings.title: GetOrder swallows all exceptions as 404, and the draft endpoint exposes the builder with no buyer binding
findings.description: GetOrderAsync uses a bare catch (lines 81-84), so database errors are returned as NotFound. CreateOrderDraftAsync (line 108) accepts a client BuyerId. The draft is computed in memory and not persisted, so impact is minor. Low confidence, listed for completeness.
findings.exploit_scenario: None significant.
findings.recommendation: Catch only KeyNotFoundException. Ignore the client BuyerId.
findings.confidence_reason: Author labels it low confidence. Swallowed exceptions and an in-memory draft are minor.

findings.title: The card number column is stored without encryption, and only the masked PAN is persisted. The CVV has no column mapping.
findings.description: PaymentMethod._cardNumber is mapped to a 25-character column. OrdersApi.cs line 107 masks the PAN to XXXX...last4 before the command is built, so only the masked value is persisted. _securityNumber is not mapped, so the CVV is not stored (I read only the PaymentMethod and Order configuration). The masking happens only in the API layer. Other callers of CreateOrderCommand, for example one that deserializes the command directly, would store the full PAN. The residual risk is low. The main exposure is the logging in F-02-05.
findings.exploit_scenario: None direct. This is a defence-in-depth note.
findings.recommendation: Perform masking in the domain or handler. Never accept a raw PAN beyond the payment provider.
findings.confidence_reason: The finding itself says only the masked PAN is stored and the CVV is not persisted. This is a missing-hardening observation.

findings.category: business logic / payment bypass by design
findings.title: PaymentProcessor does not charge anything and responds to a StockConfirmed event with OrderId only, with no amount, buyer or state verification
findings.description: The handler (lines 11-37) publishes OrderPaymentSucceeded or OrderPaymentFailed. The choice is based only on the PaymentSucceeded option (line 22 area), never on the event contents. The result event carries just the OrderId from the incoming event. Ordering therefore has no way to bind the payment confirmation to an amount or payment instrument. Together with F-07-01, any bus participant can mint a payment confirmation. This is a demo simulation, so it is flagged low.
findings.exploit_scenario: The same as F-07-01. A forged OrderPaymentSucceeded event is indistinguishable from a real one.
findings.recommendation: Replace the simulation with a real gateway and have Ordering verify the payment reference, amount and signature of the confirmation event.
findings.confidence_reason: PaymentProcessor is an intentional demo simulation. The impact depends on F-07-01.

findings.category: SSRF / path injection (low) and unauthenticated proxy
findings.title: Unauthenticated MapForwarder for /product-images/{id} with an unconstrained id substituted into the catalog-api path
findings.description: `app.MapForwarder("/product-images/{id}", "https+http://catalog-api", "/api/catalog/items/{id}/pic")` has no route constraint such as `{id:int}` and no authorization. The destination host is fixed, so this is not a classic SSRF. The id value from the URL (for example one containing encoded characters or `..`) is substituted into the internal catalog-api path, which could reach other internal catalog endpoints. Slash characters generally cannot be placed in a single route segment, so exploitability is limited. The forwarder does not attach the user token, since AddAuthToken is only on the typed HttpClients.
findings.exploit_scenario: A request such as `/product-images/1%3Fx=y` or one with dot-segments tries to reach a different internal catalog-api route through the public webapp.
findings.recommendation: Use `{id:int}` and add a request transform that rejects other values.
findings.confidence_reason: Fixed destination host, route segments cannot hold slashes, and the endpoint serves public images. Speculative with minimal impact.

findings.title: Logout is anonymous-callable and does no redirect, so the OIDC sign-out is not completed
findings.description: The `/logout` POST validates antiforgery (an exception on failure gives a 400, so CSRF is covered). It has no `.RequireAuthorization()`. It calls SignOutAsync for both the cookie and OIDC schemes without passing a RedirectUri. This looks like a functional or hardening gap rather than an exploit. Practical impact: the IdP session may persist, so the user remains logged in at the Identity provider. No attacker-controlled redirect was found. LogIn.razor builds `new Uri(ReturnUrl, UriKind.Relative)` and navigates to it. That is a relative-only URL, and open redirect is excluded from scope in any case.
findings.exploit_scenario: No concrete attack identified. The finding is low confidence and is reported only per the instruction to report when unsure.
findings.recommendation: Return a redirect with AuthenticationProperties, and require authorization on the endpoint.
findings.confidence_reason: Self-described hardening gap with CSRF covered by antiforgery and no exploit.

findings.title: Postgres uses unpinned third-party image ankane/pgvector:latest, and all databases share a single superuser
findings.description: Lines 13-15 use WithImage("ankane/pgvector") with tag "latest" and persistent lifetime. This pulls a mutable tag from a third-party Docker Hub namespace. All four databases (catalogdb, identitydb, orderingdb, webhooksdb; lines 17-20) are on one Postgres server. Every service gets a connection string through WithReference carrying the same auto-generated postgres superuser credentials. A compromise of any one service, such as the unauthenticated Catalog.API in F-09-01, gives access to the Identity DB with password hashes and to the Ordering DB. RabbitMQ is likewise shared, with one set of credentials for all services (lines 8-9).
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised service uses its own connection string to log in as postgres and read identitydb. Alternatively, a compromised or tag-replaced ankane/pgvector image runs with access to all data.
findings.recommendation: Pin the image by digest (or use the official pgvector image at a fixed tag). Create per-service database roles with least privilege, and use separate RabbitMQ users or vhosts.
findings.confidence_reason: Unpinned :latest image and a shared Postgres superuser in an Aspire dev AppHost. This is missing-hardening only.

findings.title: ESHOP_USE_HTTP_ENDPOINTS toggle switches Identity, webapp and webhooks clients to plain-HTTP launch profiles, combined with RequireHttpsMetadata=false
findings.description: ShouldUseHttpForEndpoints (AppHost.cs lines 94-102) selects the "http" profile when ESHOP_USE_HTTP_ENDPOINTS=1. identityEndpoint, then used for the Identity__Url and IdentityUrl environment variables, becomes an http URL. The OIDC code flow, cookies and tokens then travel unencrypted, and RequireHttpsMetadata=false is hardcoded in ServiceDefaults line 39 and WebApp/Extensions.cs line 82 (plus WebhookClient/Extensions.cs line 58). The comment says it is for CI and test use only, but nothing stops it from being set in a real deployment. Because it is an environment variable, I treat it as a low-confidence insecure default.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the flag is set in a deployed environment, a network-position attacker captures bearer tokens and session cookies, or tampers with the OIDC metadata.
findings.recommendation: Guard the toggle so it only takes effect when running locally. Make RequireHttpsMetadata depend on the environment.
findings.confidence_reason: ESHOP_USE_HTTP_ENDPOINTS is an env-var toggle documented for CI/test use, so it is an env-var vector and misconfiguration only.

findings.title: Auth token handler attaches the user's access token to every outgoing request from the client, with no host allow-list
findings.description: HttpClientAuthorizationDelegatingHandler.SendAsync (lines 92-104) adds `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` from the current HttpContext to every request made by a client registered with AddAuthToken. It does not check the destination host. Used by WebApp (Extensions lines 32, 36, 40) and WebhookClient (line 21). The base addresses appear to be fixed service-discovery URIs, so there is no concrete attacker-controlled host in these files. Redirects are a possible edge case: the handler runs before the inner redirect-following handler and .NET strips auth on cross-host redirects. If any code path builds a URL from user input with these clients, such as the webhook callback URL, the token leaks. I did not trace that in this focus area.
findings.exploit_scenario: Only if a future or other-area code path uses an AddAuthToken client with a user-controlled absolute URL. The attacker host receives the victim's bearer token.
findings.recommendation: Attach the token only when request.RequestUri host matches the configured service base address.
findings.confidence_reason: Speculative token leakage with no attacker-controlled host identified.

findings.title: OpenAPI document endpoint mapped in all environments when the OpenApi config section exists
findings.description: UseDefaultOpenApi calls app.MapOpenApi() (line 153) without an environment check whenever the "OpenApi" section exists. Only Scalar and the "/" redirect are gated on Development (line 155). The document is anonymous. It exposes the API surface, scopes and security schemes of Catalog, Ordering and Webhooks in production. Basket does not call UseDefaultOpenApi. Health endpoints are correctly gated to Development only (Extensions.cs lines 115-125), so there is no health exposure. The Redis key `/basket/` + `sub` (RedisBasketRepository lines 229-232) is not injectable. `sub` is a signed claim, there are no wildcard operations, and keys are binary-appended. The RabbitMQ OrderStarted handler deletes the basket for @event.UserId (handler line 14). That is only exploitable by someone who can publish to the broker, which is outside this focus area.
findings.exploit_scenario: An anonymous attacker fetches /openapi/v1.json on production services to map endpoints for further attacks.
findings.recommendation: Gate MapOpenApi to Development, or require authorization for it.
findings.confidence_reason: The OpenAPI document is exposed. This is information disclosure of low value.

findings.title: Handler logs the entire integration event object, including the user id, at Information level
findings.description: `{@IntegrationEvent}` at line 12 destructures the whole OrderStartedIntegrationEvent into the logs. The event carries UserId, and possibly more fields that I did not inspect. Low impact. Also, DeleteBasketAsync(@event.UserId) (line 14) trusts the event bus message, so broker access allows clearing any user's basket.
findings.exploit_scenario: Anyone with read access to the logs sees user ids in the event payload. An attacker with RabbitMQ publish rights can delete arbitrary users' baskets.
findings.recommendation: Log only the event id. Secure the broker with credentials and ACLs.
findings.confidence_reason: Logging a user id at Information level, and the broker-trust claim is out of scope. Noise.

findings.title: Debug-only certificate validation relaxation (trusts any cert whose Issuer is CN=localhost)
findings.description: Inside #if DEBUG (lines 117-140), the AndroidMessageHandler callback returns true if cert.Issuer equals "CN=localhost", otherwise returns errors==None. The iOS/MacCatalyst branch trusts any host starting with "https://localhost". This is gated to DEBUG builds, so it is not a production issue unless a debug build ships. The check is on the issuer only and applies to any host, so a self-signed cert with Issuer CN=localhost would be accepted for every host in a debug build.
findings.exploit_scenario: A debug build is distributed or used on a hostile network. An attacker presents a self-signed cert with Issuer "CN=localhost" for the backend host and gets a MITM position, which exposes tokens.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the exception to the request host (localhost) and verify the cert thumbprint. Make sure the code is never compiled into release builds.

findings.title: RedirectService.ExtractRedirectUriFromReturnUrl parses the redirect_uri by string splitting, but it appears unused
findings.description: The method HTML-decodes the URL, splits on "redirect_uri=", then on "signin-oidc" or "scope", and strips "&" and a few percent-encodings. It is registered in Program.cs (line 46). A grep for callers in the Identity.API controllers found none (my grep command errored on the --include glob, so this is not fully confirmed). If it is used for security decisions, the naive parsing can be fooled by a crafted returnUrl, for example a repeated redirect_uri= parameter. Given the reporting bar, I rate it low.
findings.exploit_scenario: None demonstrated. A caller that trusted this output would validate an attacker-influenced value.
findings.recommendation: Delete the unused service, or parse with QueryHelpers and validate against the client's registered redirect URIs.
findings.confidence_reason: Unused code, and the finding itself says it is unconfirmed and demonstrates no exploit.

findings.category: unsafe reflection / type resolution (reviewed, low risk)
findings.title: Outbox deserialization resolves types by name from a DB column, but only against a whitelist of entry-assembly types
findings.description: The constructor (lines 14-19) loads the entry-assembly types whose name ends with "IntegrationEvent". RetrieveEventLogsPendingToPublishAsync (lines 22-35) calls _eventTypes.FirstOrDefault(t => t.Name == e.EventTypeShortName) and then DeserializeJsonContent(type) with that type. EventTypeShortName is taken from the DB column EventTypeName. There is no Type.GetType and no polymorphic [JsonDerivedType], so there is no gadget. A DB writer can choose only among the service's own *IntegrationEvent types, and the check is by short name only. If no match is found, type is null and Deserialize throws ArgumentNullException, which breaks the publish loop for that transactionId. On the bus side, DeserializeMessage resolves eventType from the EventTypes dictionary keyed by routing key. That is a closed set, so there is no Type.GetType. The raw SQL surface in IntegrationEventLogEF is none: it uses only LINQ with parameters. OrderProcessor's raw SQL (GracePeriodOrdersRepository) is parameterised. Conclusion: no deserialization RCE found. The residual issue is that anyone who can write to the outbox table can inject arbitrary events, which the service will publish to the bus with the service's trusted identity.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker with DB write access inserts an IntegrationEventLog row. The publisher sends it onto the bus as a legitimate producer event. This only matters given an already-compromised DB.
findings.recommendation: Optional hardening. Sign outbox rows, or pin the type with an exact FullName comparison. Apply the DB least-privilege principle.
findings.confidence_reason: The finding itself says it is low risk with no gadget. Type resolution is limited to a whitelist, and exploiting it needs DB write access.

findings.category: Sensitive data handling / hardcoded payment data
findings.title: CheckoutAsync sends a hardcoded test card and ignores the user-submitted BasketCheckoutInfo card fields
findings.description: Lines 92-96 hardcode CardNumber "1111222233334444", CardHolderName "TESTUSER" and CardSecurityNumber "111", with an expiry of one year from now. The Checkout.razor form collects only address fields. BasketCheckoutInfo still declares card properties (CardNumber, CardSecurityNumber and others), and `[SupplyParameterFromForm]` binds the whole object. A client could post these extra fields, but they are ignored, so there is no real exposure. The bound fields Buyer and RequestId are attacker-settable form fields. RequestId is used as the idempotency key (`checkoutInfo.RequestId == default` check), and an attacker could reuse or choose it, which affects only themselves. Buyer is not used, because buyerId comes from the claims. This is a placeholder payment flow rather than a vulnerability, and is flagged for awareness.
findings.exploit_scenario: None directly. If real card handling is added later, the sensitive fields would be over-posted through the existing binding and the card data would be logged or stored in clear.
findings.recommendation: Use a dedicated view model with only the intended fields, and integrate a payment provider rather than passing the raw PAN and CVV through the app.
findings.confidence_reason: Hardcoded test card in a demo checkout, no real exposure. The extra form fields are ignored.
